analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license to own a handgun or semiautomatic rifle and a dealer-processed record for every sale or transfer.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2026 with no cosponsors and was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has received no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require anyone who wants to own a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle with a detachable magazine to get a federal firearm owner license — with a photo, fingerprints, and background checks — renewable every five years. Every sale or transfer of those guns would have to go through a licensed dealer who verifies the buyer's license and reports the sale to the Attorney General, creating a federal record of sale system. It also adds crimes for failing to report a lost or stolen gun, failing to update an address, and leaving a loaded gun where a child can reach it. It was introduced in the Senate with no cosponsors and referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without action.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the main beneficiaries would be communities affected by gun violence, especially communities of color that the bill's findings say suffer disproportionate gun deaths, and law enforcement, which would gain a national trail for tracing guns used in crimes. Households would gain legal pressure to store guns away from children. Gun owners who comply would gain a license, but that is a cost as much as a benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal license — a photo-ID card with an embedded fingerprint, renewed every five years and costing at most $10 in fees — required to possess a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle that takes a detachable magazine larger than 10 rounds.

Requires every sale or transfer of a covered firearm to run through a licensed dealer who verifies the buyer's license and reports the transfer to the Attorney General, creating a national record of sale intended to let police trace guns used in crime quickly.

Adds new federal crimes for failing to report a lost or stolen gun within 72 hours, failing to update an address, and leaving a loaded firearm accessible to a child who then kills or seriously injures someone — punishable by up to 10 years for licensing violations and 5 years for child-access violations.
Directs the Attorney General to build a firearm injury clearinghouse, study gun-related deaths and injuries, and study 'smart gun' technology that prevents unauthorized users from firing a weapon.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on current and future handgun and semiautomatic rifle owners, who would need to apply, submit fingerprints and mental-health certifications, pay fees up to $10, renew every five years, and route every purchase through a licensed dealer; sellers of guns privately would also lose the ability to transfer directly.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a permanent federal licensing requirement to own a handgun or semiautomatic rifle, with a photograph, fingerprints, mental-health certifications, and a criminal penalty of up to 10 years for possessing a covered firearm without a license — a significant new federal gate for an activity many Americans currently do without any license.

Applicants must certify they have not been a mental-health facility patient in the past five years and authorize release of their mental health records; prior patients need a clinician's certification that they are not a 'clear and present danger' — a standard critics argue gives examiners and the Attorney General broad, subjective discretion.

The bill repeals the statutory prohibition on establishing a federal system of firearms registration, and its record-of-sale system collects for every transfer the make, model, serial number, license number, and identities of the parties — which critics describe as a de facto national registry even though the bill states it does not authorize one.

Even private, unlicensed transfers between individuals — including most sales between neighbors or through classified ads — must first go through a licensed dealer, adding dealer fees and travel to transactions that are currently legal and free.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit — a federal licensing and trace system covering all handguns and many semiautomatic rifles, with civil liability tools and loss/theft reporting — is real but conditional on the licensing regime working as written and surviving court challenges. The costs are also real: permanent federal licensing for a right that previously required no license, criminal penalties of up to 10 years for unlicensed possession, the removal of a legal bar to building a federal registry, and a rare 'clear and present danger' mental-health standard that could function as a wide discretionary gate. There are no scoring or fiscal estimates available to weigh the costs precisely. As introduced, the burden falls on lawful owners' time, privacy, and money, while the crime-reduction benefit depends on provisions never tested at this scale.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee; with no cosponsors and no committee action since June 2026, it has not moved toward a vote.

narrative.text: The bill's entire action history is two entries on June 24, 2026: introduction in the Senate and referral to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No senator has cosponsored the bill.
The Judiciary Committee has held no markup, hearing, or vote on the bill, and it has never been scheduled on the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun owners and gun-rights groups are better off so far, since the licensing bill has gone nowhere; no one has gained the bill's benefits yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, the bill's opponents by default

for.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee; no other senator joined as a cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred and no cosponsors have signed on, so the partisan shape of support or opposition has not been tested in the record.

industries.note: Dealers become the mandatory intermediary for every private transfer of a covered firearm and must verify licenses, file transfer reports, and keep records subject to federal inspection — more business traffic but heavy compliance duties and criminal exposure for recordkeeping failures.

The bill does not ban or restrict the products themselves, so the market for covered guns continues under a licensing regime; the government gains a new window into each manufacturer's production and sales figures.
Tens of millions of existing owners of handguns and semiautomatic rifles would have to obtain a federal license within two years of enactment or face up to 10 years in prison for possession.

analysis.trajectory: A gun-licensing bill with zero cosponsors in a narrowly divided Senate referred to Judiciary has essentially no realistic path to a committee vote or floor action this Congress; the realistic expectation is that it dies quietly when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
